name: American exceptionalism
summary: American exceptionalism holds that the United States is distinctive and exemplary, founded on liberty, equality, individualism, popular government and religious faith, and that it has a special role as a beacon or leader for the world. Adherents see it as a model nation rather than one bound by Old World class divisions.
scope: The mainstream patriotic version from Winthrop and Jefferson through Tocqueville, Lipset and Reagan, in which the US is a free, religious, market-minded republic with a global leadership role. It is not a full program, so many economic and social answers are 0 or low; it excludes the Marxist and postnationalist critical senses of the term.

sources.author: Wilson Center
sources.usedFor: Anti-state individualism as a defining American trait.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Anti-statist individualism leans against state guarantees, though adherents of both parties claim the idea.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Lipset ties American distinctiveness to laissez-faire individualism, and Reagan links freedom to productive markets.

public-ownership.rationale: The American tradition described by Lipset and Reagan distrusts state ownership.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Anti-state and meritocratic values lean against higher taxes, but it is partisan.

unions-good.rationale: Lipset and Hartz note weak labor and socialist politics in the US, but adherents are split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Individual liberty and limited government in the American creed give property strong protection.

cut-welfare.rationale: The anti-state strand favors cuts but bipartisan adherents accept safety nets, so it is split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Broad free speech protection is part of the creed.

strong-leader.rationale: Constitutional government and limits on power are central; leader worship is alien.

state-harmful.rationale: Reagan says liberty contracts as government expands, yet adherents accept a constitutional state, so not extreme.

limit-guns.rationale: Constitutional-rights culture leans against it; contested.

empower-police-military.rationale: Reagan credits rebuilt defenses with peace through strength.

decide-locally.rationale: Hartz notes decentralized American government, but adherents differ on federal power.

more-religion-public.rationale: Winthrop and Reagan use religious language and Lipset notes unusual American religiosity.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Critics note historical injustices; adherents split on remedies.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Reagan warns against eradicating the American memory and urges teaching patriotism.

gradual-change.rationale: Revolutionary origin but constitutional continuity; split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Reagan celebrates open doors and the land of opportunity.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Exemptionalism and sovereignty concerns mean adherents resist ceding power to international bodies.

free-trade.rationale: Reagan celebrates free markets worldwide; trade policy is disputed.

nation-first.rationale: Exceptionalists want US leadership of the world, not retreat; the Trump strand puts America first, so split.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Obama and others frame stopping atrocities as what makes the US exceptional.

revolution-justified.rationale: The American Revolution is a founding source of the idea, per Lipset the first new nation.

central-planning.rationale: Reagan holds that democracy and free markets are productive; the idea was formed in contrast to socialism.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: America First strand supports tariffs while others oppose.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Jefferson valued yeoman farmers but adherents accept corporations.

one-party-rule.rationale: Incompatible with the republican and democratic creed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The American Revolution and Paine rejected monarchy.

democracy-best.rationale: Democracy and republican government are central to the exceptionalist claim.

direct-votes.rationale: Lipset notes populism but adherents mostly defend representative government.

natural-rulers.rationale: Egalitarian ethos is central to Lipset and Tocqueville.

separate-church-state.rationale: Religious freedom is celebrated, yet Puritan and Christian strands see a providential nation; split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion is valued, but a constitutional order is not scriptural law.

military-superiority.rationale: Reagan stresses peace through strength and proponents want the US to lead the free world.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The American nation is based on shared ideals and open to all, not ethnicity.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The idea is defined partly by the claim America lacked European class conflict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Lipset describes equality of opportunity and meritocracy rather than outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Critics cite displacement; adherents do not endorse it.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Lipset notes individualism, but Winthrop stresses mutual charity; split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Lipset describes individualism and rights consciousness as defining.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Pragmatism is a trait but ideology is also valued.

harm-principle.rationale: Libertarian strand agrees but religious and conservative strands do not.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Individualism and rights against government are central.

national-rebirth.rationale: Reagan speaks of rediscovery and renewal, not decadence as such.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Manifest destiny drove 19th-century expansion, but modern adherents mainly speak of influence, not territory.

universal-morality.rationale: Universal values of liberty are held to be for all peoples.

economic-freedom.rationale: Reagan ties liberty and prosperity together and the exceptionalist account stresses laissez-faire culture.

force-without-un.rationale: Proponents hold the US may act on its own judgment, and critics note it placed itself above international law.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Meritocratic and work ethic culture leans toward it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Absence of class conflict is a central thesis.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Reagan welcomes immigrants who embrace America, but the idea of assimilation is contested.

national-mission.rationale: Wilsonian and Cold War versions cast America as spreading liberty, but Winthrop's city on a hill and Reagan's Farewell Address beacon are exemplarist images of a model others may follow, and America First strands reject a mission abroad.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Anti-elite populism is part of the culture, but exceptionalism praises American institutions.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Inconsistent with individual rights and equality.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Critics demand accountability; adherents are split.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Skepticism of big government is shared, but most adherents accept a larger state with a strong military.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Egalitarianism is a core part of the American creed.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Critics make this claim; adherents reject it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Reagan stresses We the People telling government what it may do.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Lipset links achievement orientation and competition to American values.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Free speech tradition leans against banning parties.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Republican tradition echoes this but adherents do not address it.

separated-powers.rationale: The Constitution as limit on government is central to the American creed.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The idea is claimed by both parties, and adherents differ on how far law should limit strikes.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Reagan's optimism and the individualist creed point to opportunity rather than overpopulation as the key, though the idea is not a poverty theory.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Reagan describes a nation open to anyone with the will to come, and Lipset stresses a creed-based identity rather than shared ancestry.

party-controls-media.rationale: Liberty, including a free press, is central to the idea of the US as a model for the world.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Reagan's image of an open door for newcomers and the creed-based identity favour accessible citizenship.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Reagan's farewell speech makes patriotism and loyalty to the nation central.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Jeffersonian yeoman-farmer strand celebrates rural virtue, though modern adherents are less committed.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Populist anti-elitism runs through American self-image, but mainstream adherents also prize education; split.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Adherents are split between religious conservatives and secular liberals on school curricula.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Religious faith is part of the self-image, but adherents are split on teaching creationism.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Individualism and moral conservatism pull in opposite directions, so adherents are split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Reagan celebrates open immigration and America as a land that takes in newcomers, so descent-based citizenship is disfavoured.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Split: exceptionalists revere the Constitution's electoral college but also popular government.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Split: anti-state sentiment favours limiting central banks while others favour sound money.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The creed does not address territorial compromise; adherents split.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The tradition prizes religious liberty and a religious public culture, which Lipset and Winthrop-to-Reagan accounts stress, and rejects state control of churches.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The tradition is built on popular government and rejects hereditary or divine kingship; the founders broke from monarchy.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The tradition holds that the US was founded on liberty under law and limited government, so no ruler is above the law.

leader-cult.rationale: The tradition treats the republic as a nation of laws and equal citizens rather than of a leader, and Washington's farewell stresses principles over persons.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: The idea is defined partly by the claim that America lacked European class conflict and rejects socialism.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Religious liberty is part of the creed celebrated by Winthrop and Reagan, so punishing leaving a religion is inconsistent with it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Individual liberty is central to the creed, so state-mandated dress is rejected.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The idea rests on ideals and a founding creed, and Reagan and Winthrop treat moral vision as the driver of the nation's course.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The Constitution as limit on government and on majorities is central to the American creed.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Meritocratic and individualist strands, per Lipset, oppose quotas, though adherents are not unanimous.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Reagan celebrates free markets and open trade, and the tradition rejects autarky.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The founding rejected hereditary titles and the US Constitution forbids titles of nobility, which Lipset and Jefferson cite as marks of the nation's distinctiveness.

patriotic-education.rationale: The idea rests on pride in the nation's founding ideals, and Reagan's farewell address urges teaching patriotism to the young.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Winthrop's covenant and the founding creed in Lipset's account place a written constitution and rights at the centre of American identity.

elective-rulers.rationale: Exceptionalism is rooted in a republic founded on popular government and rejection of hereditary rule.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The founding narrative of the Declaration of Independence justifies removing rulers who violate rights and trust.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Winthrop teaches that the rich are bound to show mercy and liberality to the poor within the covenant community.

native-born-offices.rationale: Reagan celebrates the immigrant who becomes fully American; offices are open to naturalized citizens in the tradition, except the presidency.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Self-help individualism favours self-reliance, but exceptionalism also supports American leadership through aid; split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Exceptionalism treats American liberal-democratic institutions as a model with universal appeal.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Split: the religious strand of the tradition resists easy divorce while the individualist strand favours personal freedom.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Split: the anti-statist strand favours private accounts, but the tradition has accepted public pensions.

single-official-language.rationale: Split: English-only advocates cite a common civic language, while the tradition also prizes immigrant pluralism.

job-guarantee.rationale: Lipset describes distrust of the state and individualism as defining traits, which cuts against a state job guarantee.

democratic-peace.rationale: The American strand holds that spreading liberty serves peace and security, as in Wilsonian and Reagan-era policy.

non-intervention.rationale: The idea gives the US a leading role in the world, and interventions for liberty are part of the tradition.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The strand sees America as an open, free nation; conspiracy claims against a minority are not part of it.

religious-nation.rationale: The nation is defined by a civic creed of liberty open to immigrants, not by shared faith, though religion is prized.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The doctrine casts the US as a free republic that should lead as a beacon, never one that pays tribute, and Americans reject ritual submission to others.

defeat-communism.rationale: Reagan's Farewell Address and Cold War exceptionalism cast communism as a rival to the free world to be outlasted, though it is not a defining claim.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The doctrine is silent here; the anti-state strand prefers private provision, but patriotic adherents accept mixed arrangements.

religion-illusion.rationale: Winthrop's covenant and the doctrine's religious-faith theme treat religion as a lasting foundation of American life, not a consolation that fades.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The doctrine frames the nation as individualist and market-minded, with the nation-state as the unit, not communal property.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Winthrop's covenant gave a religious claim, but the mainstream view sees the US as built on ideals, not on ancestral land.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The article describes American exceptionalism as rooted in anti-colonial revolution, so ruling territories for the metropole contradicts it.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Adherents split along party lines; the idea does not address it.

assisted-dying.rationale: Adherents are split between religious conservatives and libertarian-leaning ones.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The idea does not address Islam, and adherents are split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Winthrop grounds the community in a covenant with God while the founding tradition grounds government in consent, so adherents are split.

social-market-economy.rationale: Lipset's view of American anti-statism pulls against it, but the idea is not about economic design.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Reagan's farewell stresses strength and leadership abroad, so abolishing the armed forces is rejected.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Reagan's farewell stresses strength and a leading role for the US, so staying out of blocs is contrary to the idea.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The founding rejected hereditary rule, and the American model of exceptionalism rests on a republic with elected leaders.

property-franchise.rationale: American exceptionalism holds that the nation is founded on liberty and equality and popular government; the modern strand backs universal adult suffrage.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The American creed treats free speech and a free press as real rights, defended by law and not hollowed by wealth.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The American founding celebrates government of laws, with fixed constitutional rules and independent courts, in place of arbitrary rule.

racial-franchise.rationale: Exceptionalism is built on equality and a civic, not racial, nation that welcomes immigrants; Reagan's address praises open doors.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Religious liberty is a core American ideal, so a legal limit on interfaith marriage is rejected.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Religious liberty and equality are core American ideals; shunning a minority's shops is contrary to them.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Adherents split: Jeffersonian suspicion of concentrated power coexists with Reagan-style defence of wealth creation; the idea itself does not settle it.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The idea is a view of the nation, not a social program; adherents on both sides of this issue claim it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The idea is bound up with religious faith and a free, religious republic, so state-promoted atheism is the opposite of it.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: The idea does not address it; adherents split between concern for long-term survival and scepticism of global-risk framing.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Adherents are split between the religious strand and mainstream denominations that ordain women.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Never addressed: the strand has no view, and adherents differ on how to treat the nation's past.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Split: the strand honours the fallen but in civic, not saintly, terms.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Winthrop's covenant sermon casts the colony as a godly mission and Reagan's era framed the Cold War as good against evil, though the strand is mostly civic.

god-not-male.rationale: Split: religious adherents differ on this, and it is outside the strand's core.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Winthrop's sermon and Reagan's speech frame America as a providential, religious nation, and Lipset notes its unusual religiosity.

communal-electorates.rationale: The idea rests on one citizenship, individual liberty and rejection of Old World divisions of class and creed, so religious electorates are alien to it.

free-public-college.rationale: Anti-statist individualism leans against state-funded provision, though adherents across parties split on public colleges.

arms-reduction.rationale: Reagan's farewell stresses peace through strength, and the leadership-role strand opposes cutting arms to a minimum.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Wilsonian exceptionalists favoured open covenants while realist patriots defended secret diplomacy, so adherents split.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Exceptionalism stresses national strength and duty to defend the country, so a duty to refuse war runs against patriotic military service.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The idea is a view of the nation, not an economic program, and adherents split on wage supplements.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The idea celebrates a founding constitutional order and covenant, the opposite of smashing the state; Lipset treats its liberalism as built on institutions.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Adherents prize liberty and experiment, but the idea names no stance on a free society's economic blueprint.

sacred-nation.rationale: Winthrop's covenant and the civil-religion strand treat the nation as a divinely meaningful community, though adherents locate it in ideals more than blood.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The classless, unified self-image of exceptionalism rejects the internal-exploitation analysis, which is a Marxist critique.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Law-and-order strands favour fixed sentences, but the individualist, anti-statist strand distrusts rigid rules; adherents are split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Lipset and Tocqueville stress America's religious pluralism and the absence of an established church, so no interpretation holds legal precedence.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Reagan-style limited-government adherents mostly oppose new welfare schemes, though a negative income tax has some conservative support.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Winthrop's Puritan covenant casts America as a promised land, though the idea is not about ancestral soil.

self-ownership.rationale: Lipset identifies individualism and liberty as core elements of the American creed.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The idea does not address it and adherents are split between those who see racism as largely overcome and those who do not.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The idea does not address automation and adherents are split or indifferent.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Patriotism is central, but whether it is tied to a politics for working people is contested among adherents.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The anti-state strand favors cuts but bipartisan adherents accept safety nets, so it is split. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

notes: Strands differ: the interventionist leadership strand, the America First strand and the religious strand answer differently on foreign policy and social issues. Many answers are low confidence because the idea is a view of the nation rather than a full program.
